This is a layman's guess on my part: because we have yet to see definitive proof first its existence, the odds are equal going either way. Sorry if I muddled that up, going on 24 hours now. Cheers!

No, we don't. The reason it's called "Dark Matter" in the first place, is because we can't see it, have no evidence of it's composition, and generally just some wild speculation on what it might be. All we know is, it interacts gravitationally.

There are several propositions for what this dark matter may actually be. Particle physics theories that extend the standard models are wonderful sources for potential dark matter candidate particles (the so-called "WIMPS", weakly interacting massive particles). The problem is that there is quite a number of these theories, and getting some conclusive observational quantities that would allow us to tell the nature of these particles apart is difficult.

Anothe possibility would be "MACHOS", massive compact halo objects, which would be something like free-flying black holes that are not gravitationally bound to any solar system, and not accreting mass strongly (thus not emitting any radiation). There is, however, a complete lack of evidence for any of those ever strinking normal matter (which would make it light up) or gravitational microlensing they would produce.

Or it might just be normal matter afterall, that we just don't see for a bizarre reason that nobody has thought of yet.

So as long as we don't know, we'll keep calling it "Dark Matter" and hope that some explanation eventually comes up.
